_comment: Authored cases that are not one of the 64 lever fixtures. Kept OUT of learn.json so
that file stays byte-identical to the pre-build state and the fixture-preservation
PROVENANCE. The accuracy-brief case is Sourced, and its source is THIS COLLECTION'S OWN
BUILD RECORD — it happened while these demos were being built and is written down in the
project's record. It is deliberately NOT presented as a general research finding about
prompting, and the figures below are quoted as what this project's own research lane
recorded, not as independently verified facts about the world. That distinction is the
whole reason the card is credible: it is first-party testimony about a documented event,
and overreaching it into a general claim would repeat the exact error it describes.

accuracyBrief.kickerQual: this project's own build record, 2026-09-16 — a first-party account, not a general finding
accuracyBrief.eyebrow: A real prompt, from building this collection
accuracyBrief.title: Every sentence was true. The answer was still wrong.
setup: These demos were built by AI agents working from written briefs. One brief carried a reasonable-sounding instruction: **make it 100% accurate.**
Nobody lied. Every claim that came back checked out — the citations resolved, the numbers matched their sources, the corrections were real corrections.
And the overall picture it painted was **wrong**. Asked to survey how fast AI was improving, the work came back reading as though not much had changed.

tell.text: The tell, from the record: the research found the cost of one benchmark task had fallen roughly **16,000-fold** — from about $4,560 to about $0.284 — while accuracy rose. That got one clause. Four small qualifications about wording got a full paragraph.
tell.note: Those figures are quoted from this project's own research file, which is where the episode is recorded. They are cited here as what that lane reported, not as a number this demo independently verified.

check.question: The instruction was “make it 100% accurate”, and every individual claim was accurate. So what went wrong?
check.prompt: This is the same machinery as the three levers, running in a direction that is harder to see.

options.label: The prompt only asked for one kind of finding, so it only got one kind back
options.feedback: That is it. “Don't overstate” is a one-directional instruction: it rewards catching an exaggeration and pays nothing for catching an understatement. Every sentence can be true while the selection of sentences is misleading. The repair is not less care — it is symmetry: ask for the strongest well-sourced case in both directions, and make the answer say which way the evidence actually falls.

options.label: Whoever wrote the brief was careless, and a more precise instruction would have fixed it
options.feedback: It is the tempting answer and it is wrong here. The brief was careful — that is what makes the case worth teaching. Precision was never the missing ingredient; the missing ingredient was the second direction. A more precisely worded one-directional instruction returns a more precise one-directional answer.

options.label: The answers were false, and better fact-checking would have caught it
options.feedback: This is the flawed model the case exists to break. Fact-checking works sentence by sentence, and every sentence passed. A failure of selection is invisible at claim level: you cannot catch it by checking what is there, only by asking what the prompt never asked for.

options.label: Pulling another lever — more context, or a tighter success spec — would have fixed it
options.feedback: Careful: this is the demo's own lesson misapplied, and noticing that is the point of putting this card last. The three levers make an answer better aimed. They do not audit what the request quietly selected for. A lever fixes a vague request; nothing here fixes a request that was specific in one direction only.

accuracyBrief.takeaway: A request shapes the answer even when every sentence in the answer is true. Ask what your prompt is quietly selecting for — and ask for both directions.
